{{short description|Graph nodes linked to, but not part of, a subgraph}}
{{one source |date=April 2024}}
In [[graph theory]], the '''outer boundary''' of a subset {{mvar|S}} of the [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] of a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] {{mvar|G}} is the set of vertices in {{mvar|G}} that are adjacent to vertices in {{mvar|S}}, but not in {{mvar|S}} themselves. The '''inner boundary''' is the set of vertices in {{mvar|S}} that have a neighbor outside {{mvar|S}}. The '''edge boundary''' is the set of edges with one endpoint in the inner boundary and one endpoint in the outer boundary.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Benjamini | first = Itai
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-02576-6
 | isbn = 978-3-319-02575-9
 | page = 2
 | publisher = Springer | location = Cham
 | series = Lect. Notes Math.
 | title = Coarse geometry and randomness: École d'Été de Probabilités de Saint-Flour XLI – 2011
 | volume = 2100
 | year = 2013}}</ref>

These boundaries and their sizes are particularly relevant for [[Cheeger constant (graph theory)|isoperimetric problems in graphs]], [[planar separator theorem|separator theorems]], [[minimum cut]]s, [[expander graph]]s, and [[percolation theory]].
